entries.title: FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Gianni Infantino
entries.summary: Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.
entries.content:
Switzerland

FIFA warns against 'concerted effort' to undermine Infantino

August 9, 2026

Pressure is mounting on the FIFA president Gianni Infantino after plans to sell a stake in the World Cup collapsed and fresh allegations emerged relating to his time at UEFA.

FIFA warned against what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

The statement, issued late on Saturday, comes amid a growing dispute over Infantino's leadership after the failed plan to create a subsidiary to run the men's World Cup and other events, with up to a 20% stake offered to external investors.

The proposal drew criticism from European governing body UEFA, which threatened to boycott future World Cups, as well as several national associations and senior FIFA officials, and prompted calls for Infantino to resign.

Amid the growing criticism Infantino persuaded FIFA's Board of Management to express its full support for him at a crisis meeting in Rabat, Morocco, on Wednesday. 

Report raises new questions over Infantino

The pressure on Infantino intensified on Friday when British newspaper the Daily Telegraph reported a six-figure sum was paid to a female employee alleged to have been in a relationship with him during his time as UEFA general secretary.

UEFA confirmed a departure payment and said it also funded her MBA course, stating both were in line with regulations at the time.

A FIFA spokesman told the Telegraph on Friday: "FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue."

Responding to the latest scrutiny, FIFA said on Saturday, without directly mentioning the Telegraph report, "recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its President."

Investment plan dispute deepens leadership crisis

The fallout over the shelved private investment plan has overshadowed Infantino's bid for a fourth term as FIFA president.

After this week's crisis meeting, UEFA said it no longer has confidence in him, and Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness called for his resignation.

Despite the controversy, Infantino retains strong backing among FIFA members, with the Confederation of African Football (CAF) unanimously supporting his leadership and South American governing body CONMEBOL opposing any attempt to remove him without a vote of all member associations.

FIFA said that those who lacked the support of its member associations should not seek to achieve "allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA's established democratic processes."

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare
entries.summary: German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Interior Minister warns of 'daily' hybrid warfare

August 9, 2026

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt says attacks by foreign powers have become a constant threat to Germany. His remarks come just days after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig airport.

Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt on Sunday warned that hybrid warfare attacks had become a daily threat to the country.

"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said.

He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats.

A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, Dobrindt said. 

Drones spotted above military base in west Germany

On Saturday, Germany's armed forces confirmed that two drones had been spotted late on Thursday over a German military base in Mechernich in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia near the Belgian border.

The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said.

German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks.

Drone incident at Leipzig airport

The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario."

While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022.

On Friday, the Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation" and said Russia was once more being accused of hostile actions "without the slightest evidence being presented."

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Nigeria marries 1,500 couples in mass wedding
entries.summary: The government describes the program as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability. Among those married were people who lost family members in violent attacks.
entries.content:
Nigeria

Nigeria marries 1,500 couples in mass wedding

August 9, 2026

The government describes the program as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability. Among those married were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

Some 1,500 couples got married at a mass wedding organized by Abba Kabir Yusuf, the governor of Kano state, in northern Nigeria.

The regional government described the two-day event as a way to support low-income families and promote social stability.

"The whole idea for the marriage is to help our families and we husbands who are not financially stable to marry; that's why the government is helping us get married," groom Abubakar Aliyu Musa told the Associated Press.

This is the second time Yusuf's administration has organized a mass wedding.

What else do we know about the program in Kano state?

According to Kano's regional government, each bride received a dowry of 200,000 naira ($147, €127) and support to set up a small business.

The couples were also given household items including beds, mattresses and blankets.

The couples underwent screening and counseling before the wedding.

Governor Yusuf described the program as a "bold social intervention aimed at restoring hope and supporting dignified family life in Kano."

"The program was designed not only to assist women who might otherwise struggle to afford marriage, but also to strengthen families and promote social stability in the state," he said.

Widower remarries in mass wedding

Among those who participated in the mass wedding were people who lost family members in violent attacks.

One of them was Haruna Bashir, who lost his wife and six children in an attack earlier in the year. Daurawa hailed the ceremony as a step toward Bashir "gradually returning to normal life" after having "hardly interacted with people … since the tragic incident."

Nigeria has been grappling with a major security crisis for years, particularly in the country's north, which is regularly hit by raids and attacks by Islamist insurgents and organized gangs.

Many armed groups in Nigeria also kidnap schoolchildren to demand large ransoms.

On Wednesday, the Nigerian government announced the release of 308 people who had been abducted.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Kosovo PM Kurti egged in parliament amid political crisis
entries.summary: Kosovo has held three elections in over two years. Albin Kurti's ruling Vetevendosje is struggling to garner the two-thirds majority required to elect a president.
entries.content:
Kosovo

Kosovo PM Kurti egged in parliament amid political crisis

August 8, 2026

Kosovo has held three elections in over two years. Albin Kurti's ruling Vetevendosje is struggling to garner the two-thirds majority required to elect a president.

Kosovo's parliament was suspended on Saturday after an opposition lawmaker threw eggs at caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti.

"Shame on you!" Time Kadrijaj of the conservative opposition Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) party shouted in parliament before hurling eggs at Kurti.

In response, Kurti said that he was "happy to pay this price" if it was the cost of dialogue.

Kurti's left-wing Vetevendosje (VV) party is known for its own parliamentary disruptions, with party representatives launching tear gas in the chamber in 2018 and also on multiple occasions in 2015.

What is the political situation in Kosovo?

The incident comes after days of negotiations as Kurti attempts to gain enough opposition support to elect a new president amid Kosovo's broader political crisis.

The Balkan country has held three elections in over two years.

Kurti achieved his parliamentary majority with ethnic minority MPs in a December election that followed an inconclusive vote in February 2025.

His VV party's share of the vote fell from 51% to 43% in a snap election in June, but it maintained a parliamentary majority alongside ethnic minority allies.

However, Kurti requires a two-thirds majority in parliament to elect a president.

The current negotiations seem to have ground to another stalemate, with neither side having agreed to a candidate.

A constitutional deadline to elect a speaker of parliament expired on Friday. Opposition lawmakers have threatened legal action over Kurti's request for more time to negotiate.

Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008 after the 1998-99 war, which ended with Serbia's withdrawal following a NATO bombing campaign.

Kosovo has been recognized by over half of the world's countries, including the United States and most European Union countries.

Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Thousands attend Prague Pride parade
entries.summary: Participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the CSD parade in Berlin. The march was accompanied by enhanced security measures.
entries.content:
Czech Republic

Thousands attend Prague Pride parade

August 8, 2026

Participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the CSD parade in Berlin. The march was accompanied by enhanced security measures.

Tens of thousands of people marched through Czech capital of Prague on Saturday as part of LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations.

The festival is to last for a week. The theme of this year's event is "Times are changing."

At the start of the parade, participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the Cristopher Street Day (CSD) parade in Berlin two weeks ago.

The July 25 attack killed one person and injured around 31 others.

The Saturday march in Prague was accompanied by enhanced security measures, including the deployment of hundreds of police officers and a de-escalation team.

Participants were also told to carry banners by hand or to use plastic poles rather than wooden poles.

"As every year, the aim of the festival is to raise awareness of LGBT+ issues, to show how this community lives in the Czech Republic and that it is still waiting for equal rights," the director of Prague Pride, Kamila Frohlichova, was cited by Germany's DPA news agency as saying.

What else do we know about the Pride march in Prague?

According to police reports, there were no major incidents.

A group of counter-demonstrators also gathered along part of the march's trajectory.

The march began at Wenceslas Square in central Prague around noon (10:00 UTC/GMT) and arrived at Stvanice island in the Vltava River that passes through the city at around 2:30 p.m. local time, according to Czech media.

A musical program was held once the march reached its terminus and the festivities continued into the night.

entries.title: US Senate confirms Trump loyalist Todd Blanche as new AG
entries.summary: Republicans dropped their opposition and confirmed President Donald Trump's former defense lawyer to a Cabinet position. Now, Todd Blanche will act as the nation's top law enforcement officer.
entries.content:
United States of America

US Senate confirms Trump loyalist Todd Blanche as new AG

August 8, 2026

Republicans dropped their opposition and confirmed President Donald Trump's former defense lawyer to a Cabinet position. Now, Todd Blanche will act as the nation's top law enforcement officer.

The US Senate has narrowly approved President Donald Trump's nominee for the job of attorney general, making Todd Blanche the nation's top law enforcement officer in an early morning vote on Saturday.

The Republican-controlled body delivered a 50-49 vote to confirm the controversial Trump loyalist.

Louisiana Republican Bill Cassidy was the last-minute convert this time, supplying the crucial deciding vote after his colleagues Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine jumped ship to join the chamber's Democrats in voting against Blanche's appointment.

In explaining her opposition, Murkowski said the country was in need of an attorney general "who will check the worst impulses of this administration."

On the Senate floor, Cassidy outlined his own conversion, saying he believed Blanche's relationship with Trump would make him effective at pushing back against Trump's demands.

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who was Trump's personal defense lawyer and had been serving as acting attorney general since April, wrote on X, "I am deeply honored by the trust and confidence President Trump has placed in me to lead the Department of Justice as our great nation's 88th attorney general."

Senators question whether Blanche will be nation's lawyer, or Trump's

There is great concern that Trump sees Blanche as "his lawyer," something that he has often openly expressed the need for in the position of attorney general, which is supposed to be independent.

"The attorney general is supposed to be the people's lawyer," Illinois Democratic Senator Dick Durbin said during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday.

"Mr. Blanche," added Durbin, the Committee's ranking Democrat, "continues to operate as the president's personal lawyer, treating the Justice Department like a law firm serving one client — the president."

On Saturday, Durbin said it would be a "serious mistake" to give Blanche control at the DOJ, "If there is ever a moment in history when we need an attorney general above reproach, who is clearly dedicated to ending corruption, even at the highest level of our government, it's right now."

During his time in office, Trump has often railed against attorneys general for not being aggressive enough in pursuing his agenda — most often when it is tied to retribution against his political opponents.

Jeff Sessions, Bill Barr and Pam Bondi all fell out of the president's good graces for failing to fully satisfy his legal desires.

Blanche is seen as a staunch ally who has no qualms doing the president's bidding.

Blanche won votes by promising to scrap '1776 fund' and Trump tax immunity scheme

Blanche previously defended Trump against criminal charges over the falsification of business records with the intent of hiding an affair with an adult movie actress, as well as another for the mishandling of classified documents in his attempt to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election.

Both cases were dropped after Trump won reelection in 2024.

During his time at the DOJ, Blanche has handled portions of the case against deceased sex offender and presidential friend Jeffrey Epstein — most prominently overseeing the release of millions of documents tied to the case, as well as the transfer of Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell to a more comfortable, minimum-security federal prison in Texas after he personally met with her.

Under Blanche and his predecessor Bondi, the DOJ has lost thousands of employees through firing, resignation or voluntary departure.

Blanche's candidacy was vehemently opposed by Democrats, and even some Republican lawmakers had qualms with his avoidance of forthright answers about a dubious $1.776 billion (€1.5 billion) compensation fund for presidential political allies — including those who stormed the US Capital on January 6, 2021 — accusing the federal government of unfair treatment; and DOJ directives that would see the president, his two eldest sons and the Trump Organization shielded from tax audits and penalties for life.

Two retiring Republican senators, John Cornyn (Texas) and Thom Tillis (North Carolina), had loudly proclaimed that they would vote against Blanche's appointment unless the compensation fund was dropped.

He assured them that it would be, while also saying that the Trumps' tax immunity would only be applied "retroactively" and not to future filings, clearing the way for Saturday's confirmation vote.

entries.title: Ukraine: Russia pounds Kyiv as Zelenskyy visits Serbia
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is visiting Serbia, a country that has traditionally been friendly with Moscow, as Russia strikes the Kyiv region once again.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Russia pounds Kyiv as Zelenskyy visits Serbia

August 8, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is visiting Serbia, a country that has traditionally been friendly with Moscow, as Russia strikes the Kyiv region once again.

As Russia continues its relentless bombardment of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia, a European country that has maintained friendly relations with Russia despite the latter's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Zelenskyy arrived in Belgrade Friday evening and had dinner with his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vucic. They met again for talks at the presidential palace on Saturday.

Later, Zelenskyy wrote on X that he and Vucic had discussed ways to strengthen infrastructure in both countries, including ports and railways, as well as economic development, reconstruction, and job creation in Ukraine and Serbia.

Representatives from both countries signed a memorandum of understanding regarding agricultural and food safety cooperation.

Zelenskyy added that the leaders also discussed the challenges of the upcoming winter in Ukraine, heavily hit by ⁠Russian attacks on energy facilities, and relations with the European Union. He also thanked Vucic for a new package of humanitarian support for Ukraine.

Serbia supports Ukraine's territorial integrity

Vucic said that Serbia will continue to support Ukraine's independence and territorial integrity, including the territories that Russia has seized since 2014.

"You have never heard a single bad word about our country, not from Volodymyr Zelenskyy nor anyone else in Ukraine, and I am extremely grateful to our Ukrainian friends for that," Vucic said.

The remark appeared to address the fact that Ukraine refuses to recognize Kosovo's independence, which was declared in 2008. Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia.

Vucic said he was skeptical that either Serbia or Ukraine would quickly join the European Union. However, he added that Belgrade would support Kyiv's bid.

Serbia has repeatedly refused to put sanctions on Moscow. This has angered the EU and delayed Belgrade's path to joining the bloc.

Both leaders also said their countries want to improve economic cooperation and finalize a free trade agreement by the end of the year. ​

Despite its dependence on Russian energy, Serbia has supplied nonmilitary aid to Ukraine. The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, but Vucic has denied this claim.

Vucic traveled to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and again this year. Despite pledging aid to Ukraine, he has refrained from signing a formal declaration of support for Ukraine in the war.

Russian attacks on Kyiv continue while Kyiv strikes Russian refineries

The meeting came after at least four people, including a child, were killed in overnight Russian air attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, and the surrounding region, officials said on Saturday.

"Last night, Russia killed three people in Pukhivka, Kyiv region, with drone strikes," Zelenskyy wrote on X. He added that the victims were a grandfather, a grandmother and their 3-year-old grandson.

Authorities said three other members of the family and a neighbor who came to their aid were hospitalized.

At least one more person was killed in Kyiv in a strike involving six ballistic missiles against civilian infrastructure, according to Zelenskyy.

Ukraine's air force reported downing or intercepting 135 of the 151 drones that Russia launched overnight.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff announced that the military had attacked Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries overnight, resulting in fires at both locations.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Iran war: IRGC says Hormuz to open if US accepts Iran's terms
entries.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said the reopening of the vital Strait of Hormuz did not depend on the outcome of ongoing talks with Oman. DW has more.
entries.content:
Iran

IRGC says Hormuz to open if US accepts Iran's terms

Published August 8, 2026last updated August 8, 2026

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said the reopening of the vital Strait of Hormuz did not depend on the outcome of ongoing talks with Oman. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The Revolutionary Guard says Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz once the US 'corrects its behavior' and accepts Iran's conditions
  • They include never threatening Iran again, lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets
  • The Guards also say the strategic waterway's reopening does not depend on how talks with Oman develop
  • Iran says the talks are nearing their 'final' stages, with Oman calling the discussions 'positive'
  • The UAE says Iran targeted tanker transiting in Hormuz

Keep reading for the latest developments on the conflict in the Middle East on Saturday, August 8, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

What are Iran's demands in negotiations with the US?

Earlier, we reported that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said talks with the US on reopening the Strait of Hormuz depend on Washington "compensating" Iran for the US "violation" of a June memorandum of understanding the two nations signed.

Aragchi and the IRGC had also pointed to "other conditions" that would need to be met.

Iran's Supreme National Security Council said the country would not lift its blockade of Hormuz until the US "corrects its behavior."

In a statement by the council's secretary and Revolutionary Guard commander Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr that was published on Iran's state broadcaster, Iran said the US must:

  • Never threaten Iran again
  • Permanently end its war against Iran and its allies in the region, namely Lebanese militants Hezbollah; Houthi rebels in Yemen; and Hamas in the Gaza Strip
  • Lift its blockade of Iranian ports and ships in the Strait of Hormuz and pull its military out of the area
  • Lift sanctions and release frozen Iranian assets 

The US has yet to respond.

Skip next section WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

WATCH: Iran and Oman near landmark shipping agreement

Iran says it is in the final stages of reaching an agreement with Oman on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Reports suggest the deal would give Tehran oversight of vessels entering the Persian Gulf, while Oman would manage outbound traffic.

If finalized, the arrangement could mark a significant shift in regional influence and raise questions about freedom of navigation, security, and the balance of power in the Gulf.

DW spoke to analyst Megan Sutcliffe and former US diplomat Alan Eyre, who helped negotiate the 2015 Iran nuclear deal, about what this could mean for the region and beyond.

Skip next section Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defense deal raises new security questions

On Friday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan unveiled a new security alliance that bears strong similarities to NATO's principles of collective defense.

The three regional powers — who are also strategic allies of the US — have signed a defense pact that is "intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression."

The deal is widely viewed as the three Sunni-majority nations' way of defending themselves against the rising threat from an increasingly hostile Iran, where Shiite Islam is the state religion.

The agreement could also be seen as a sign of shifting power dynamics in the region, as well as a way to hedge against an unreliable US, amid uncertainty over its long-term commitment to its role in enforcing security in the Gulf.

DW's Brent Goff spoke to experts Dania Thafer and Kamran Bokhari to learn more about what the new agreement means for the region and the US-Iran conflict.

Skip next section Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman calls Hormuz talks 'positive,' warns against attacks

Oman's Foreign Ministry on Saturday said talks with Iran about the future of maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz were "proceeding in a positive and constructive atmosphere."

But Muscat warned against "repeated attacks" on cargo ships, which it said could jeopardize the negotiations, although it stopped short of explicitly naming Iran.

Tehran has been targeting ships it says have ties with the US or that fail to comply with its orders.

Earlier on Saturday, Iran said talks over a deal with Oman were "approaching the final stages."

Skip next section IN DEPTH: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?

IN DEPTH: How viable is the potential Iran-Oman Hormuz shipping deal?

Iran says a shipping accord with Oman is in its final stages, but analysts warn sanctions, security concerns and rival US and Iranian goals could limit its impact.

Learn more about the potential deal between Iran and Oman in this report.

Skip next section WATCH: Will Iran develop a nuclear weapon?

WATCH: Will Iran develop a nuclear weapon?

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he is determined to prevent what he says are Iran's plans to build nuclear weapons. But is there any evidence that Iran plans to build up its nuclear capabilities?

Skip next section UAE accuses Iran of attacking state-owned ship in Hormuz

UAE accuses Iran of attacking state-owned ship in Hormuz

The United Arab Emirates on Saturday accused Iran of attacking a tanker belonging to its state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) while the vessel was sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement, the UAE's Foreign Ministry slammed what it called a "hostile" missile attack. No casualties were caused, the statement added.

The ministry also accused Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) of "acts of piracy" by attacking commercial cargo ships and using the strait to exert economic pressure on the US and its allies in the region.

The IRGC has warned it would target ships with ties to Tehran's enemies transiting the waterway or if they fail to comply with Iran's orders, such as paying a fee to pass through the Iranian naval blockade.

On Friday, ADNOC — one of the world's biggest energy producers and exporters — said Iran had attacked 15 of its ships with missiles and drones since the conflict started in late February, "including three vessels this week alone."

Iran has targeted a range of countries in the Middle East region that have ties with the US in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes.

Skip next section Iran says US must agree to its terms before it reopens Hormuz

Iran says US must agree to its terms before it reopens Hormuz

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said Saturday that Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz after the United States agrees to its terms.

On Friday, an American official said progress in talks between Iran and Oman could lead to the reopening of the strait. Hormuz has been largely closed to maritime traffic for months as Iran and the US each impose their own blockades.

While Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday said talks with Oman were nearing their "final stages," he warned that progress was "not a sign" that the strait's reopening was imminent.

"The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is subject to other conditions and compensation for the violation of the memorandum of understanding by the United States," Araghchi said, referring to a June agreement between Washington and Tehran.

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, reported that Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said that Hormuz's reopening "is subject ​to the specific mechanisms ​and conditions of the ​Islamic Republic of Iran ‌and is not related to ​the ⁠negotiations between Iran and Oman."

"The enemy is forced to accept Iran's conditions for the opening of the strait and to refrain from the interference that it is currently making in the negotiations — which have almost reached their end — between Iran, Oman and other countries," Mohebbi said.

Traffic through the strait, which was the conduit for 20% of the world's oil and gas before the war, has been severely restricted since the war began five months ago.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has said that Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz on the condition that the United States accepts its terms in full.

The Guards have also said ongoing talks with Oman, its neighbor across the strait, would not have any bearing on whether Tehran lifts its blockade of Hormuz.

The UAE said Saturday that one of its tankers was targeted while trying to sail through the strait.

We will bring you more on these stories and more on the war between the US and Iran and the rest of the region.

entries.title: War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque?
entries.summary: Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

War, terror, diplomacy: What if Israel takes Al-Aqsa Mosque?

August 8, 2026

Reports from Jerusalem suggest that Israeli authorities are taking over one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque. If they do, experts say anything could happen, from war to terrorism to ending diplomatic ties.

The statement issued after this week's meeting in Jordan was blunt about what might happen next.

Israeli infringements on one of Islam's holiest sites, the Al-Aqsa Mosque in east Jerusalem, could lead to "a religious conflict with repercussions that will extend beyond the region and threaten regional and international peace and security," the foreign ministers of 10 countries belonging to the Arab League said after Wednesday's emergency meeting in Amman, Jordan. The statement was also signed by ministers from Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, and Malaysia.

Jordan's foreign minister called the meeting because of mounting evidence that the Israeli government is surreptitiously changing a decades-old agreement meant to ensure intercommunal peace at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, an area of great religious significance to Muslims, Jews, and Christians.

"We warn that tampering with the status quo … could trigger a religious conflict that will reverberate beyond Palestine and Jordan into the whole Muslim world," Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi told the UK newspaper the Guardian before the meeting.

Israel's Foreign Ministry issued a response, saying the statement was inaccurate and Jerusalem "has never been more open and accessible to worshippers of all faiths."

Why is Al-Aqsa such a big issue?

Al-Aqsa is considered the third-holiest site in Islam, after Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia. The compound, also known as the Temple Mount, is also Judaism's holiest site — two Jewish temples are thought to have stood there — and it is also of significance to Christians for its biblical connections to Jesus Christ's life.

Al-Aqsa also bears a lot of political weight because the mosque is seen by many as the embodiment of Palestinian identity, a flashpoint in a city sought as the capital of any eventual Palestinian state.

Because of the site's importance, when Israel first occupied East Jerusalem in 1967, it was deemed in the interests of Israeli national security to keep allowing Muslims to worship there. Jews could only visit and would not be allowed to pray there. Instead Jewish visitors perform religious rituals at the wall below the mosque, known as the Western or Wailing Wall.

Jordan was also allowed to continue its century-old custodianship of the site, and today the mosque is administered by a religious trust called the Islamic Waqf, paid for by Jordan at about $20 million (€17 million) annually. Israeli authorities still take care of security there.

This delicate compromise is known as the "status quo." But recent reports indicate that the situation has been changing.

Residents of Jerusalem say dozens of mosque officials employed by Jordan have been prevented from entering Al-Aqsa this year.

The number of Muslim worshipers halved during 2025, according to Jerusalem-based monitors. More Jewish worshipers are being allowed in and are increasingly overtly performing rituals, something forbidden for decades, including by Jewish religious authorities. The Times of Israel reported in January that police openly let Jewish visitors take printed prayer sheets onto the site for the first time.

In June, there were also reports of an Israeli-US plan to turn the mosque area into a "multifaith center," although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio later denied any knowledge of such a plan.

Why is this happening now?

This is not the first time that the governments of Muslim-majority countries and activists in Jerusalem have issued such warnings.

For decades, Jewish fringe groups, often referred to as the Temple Mount movement, have demanded that they be allowed to pray at the site. The most extremist of these groups say they want to demolish the mosque and construct a new Jewish temple.

At first they were mostly ignored, Jerusalem-based lawyer Daniel Seidemann wrote in 2025. Seidemann is the founder of Terrestrial Jerusalem, an organization that tracks such developments in the city. But, he said, that "radical fringe" has become more mainstream. "Over time, the Temple Mount movements, backed by more than 100 rabbis associated with the settler movement in the West Bank, became more visible, more vocal and more provocative," Seidemann said.

"This crisis has been decades in the making," said Omar Rahman, a fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs. "There's been an effort from religious extremists to destroy the Al-Aqsa Mosque since at least the 1980s, when plots to do that were uncovered. But those groups and those ideologies have gained more representation within the Israeli [parliament] Knesset today."

An October 2025 report by the Ir Amim Association, which focuses on Israeli-Palestinian issues in Jerusalem, found that politicians, including from within Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's national-conservative Likud party, frequently break rules around the Al-Aqsa status quo but never face consequences from authorities.

"In practice, Netanyahu allows and normalizes grave breaches of the status quo," the association reported. Yet Netanyahu "continues to declare that his government remains committed to the status quo and nothing has changed."

What happens if erosion of Al Aqsa status quo continues?

"It would be very unwise to make any sort of prediction," Joost Hiltermann, a special adviser for the Middle East and North Africa at the Crisis Group think tank, told DW.

But, Hiltermann said, it's essential to consider that "while the fate of Jerusalem as a city may be an overriding Palestinian concern, the fate of the holy sites of Islam in Jerusalem is an abiding global Muslim concern. Not just for the Arab world but also for the largest Muslim countries: Indonesia, Pakistan, Bangladesh. So any Israeli attempt to change the status quo would face a global backlash."

In the past, changes have led to violence. In 2000, Ariel Sharon, an Israeli right-wing opposition leader at the time, visited Al-Aqsa — an event that was seen as one reason for the Palestinian uprising known as the Second Intifada. In 2017, when Israeli authorities erected cameras and metal detectors at the site, it led to deadly protests.

One likely outcome of further infringements of the status quo would be major public protests in Muslim-majority countries. "While the Arab regimes would be reluctant to engage in any sort of confrontation with Israel, their publics will be outraged," Hiltermann said. "The regimes will have to manage that, and they will try to do so by launching vigorous criticism of Israel, not followed by any action — they've become very good at that. The same will be true for Indonesia and others. But all of them may have a hard time controlling domestic fury."

Rahman said the  consequences of further Israeli infringement would depend on how radically things changed at Al-Aqsa. "It would trigger a fairly significant reaction, but the extent of it is hard to say," he said. "It could spark a catastrophic religious war or maybe just a diplomatic reaction, or maybe it simply adds to the well of grievance against Israel," he added.

Because Al Aqsa is so important in Islam, it could also make it hard for some countries to resist an upsurge in anti-Israel feeling, even if they might want to, he adds. For example, countries like Morocco and the United Arab Emirates that normalized relations with Israel might feel forced to reverse that.

Because of Al Aqsa's significance to Palestinian identity, the Gaza-based militant group Hamas often says it is defending the mosque. Extremist groups with an Islamist background have also used defense of Al Aqsa to recruit members.

Edited by: M Gagnon

entries.title: Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border
entries.summary: A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said. Bulgaria summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.
entries.content:
Bulgaria

Bulgaria: Unknown drone explodes near Romanian border

August 8, 2026

A drone that entered Bulgaria's airspace exploded near the Romanian border and the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, the Bulgarian prime minister said. Bulgaria summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning.

According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania. He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone.

Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine.

"We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said.

What do we know about the drone?

Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his Cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was.

However, he said it was believed the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced.

When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type.

After analysing the debris, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was of a type "widely used by the Ukrainian military." According to the AFP news agency, Bulgaria also summoned the Ukrainian ambassador for consultations.

Kyiv said it was "in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances" of the incident, the latest case of a drone straying into NATO airspace as Ukraine fights off Russia's invasion.

"We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria," Ukraine's foreign ministry spokesman Georgiy Tykhyi said.

Radev said the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size.

Drone incidents on rise in EU countries

In recent months, there have been an increasing number of incidents involving drones in Eastern European countries that are both EU and NATO members and that support Ukraine in its four-and-a-half-year war against Russia's invasion.

The origin of the drone that exploded in Bulgaria and its potential connection to Russia or Ukraine are still unclear. Radev said that teams from the Bulgarian border police and the Ministry of Defense are working to determine the origin of the drone.

Bulgaria's Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said the incident would be raised at a meeting of the North Atlantic Council early next week.

Romania, which borders Ukraine, has faced frequent drone incursions, including crashes on its territory, such as a May incident in which a drone struck an apartment building.

Earlier this week in Germany, an explosive-laden drone was defused at Leipzig Airport, in what Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt called a "new level of danger."

Edited by: Rana Taha
